addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

# Todo

This file uses [Prose form](AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains near term tasks with a short description and
uses links or reference links for more details.

## In Progress

When a `## Todo` item is picked up, its text moves here: the
problem overview and its list of things to do. That is followed
by the "plan" — a bulleted list of the development "ladder":
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-0 blah (done)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-1 blah blah (current)
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y-2 blah blah blah
   - [[N]] 0.xx.y close-out and validation

**feat: grade the run from raw batches**

The 0.23.0 cycle, decided in
[Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity and
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway, while the calibration-time
grade certified the room, not the exam. Drop the adjustment
machinery; grade the run from its own time-ordered batches.

- [[67]] 0.23.0-0 `chore: open raw-batch grading cycle`
  (done)
- [[68]] 0.23.0-1 `feat: micro-probe inner-loop sizing`
  (done) —
  `pick_inner` inputs from a ~1 ms micro-probe (low quantile
  over back-to-back timer pairs), never printed; unhooks
  sizing from `cfg.overhead`
- [[69]] 0.23.0-2 `feat: time-ordered batch pipeline`
  (done) —
  samples land in a raw batch buffer; per-batch summaries
  (floor, mean, census counts) taken as batches fill, then
  bulk-record into the histogram; bounded memory
- [[70]] 0.23.0-3 `feat: batch-based run gauge` (done) — relocate
  the -6 grade machinery (signals, thresholds, letter) onto
  batch summaries: drift from floor movement, bursts localized
  in time, interference rate from census counts (absorbs the
  crossover entry's rate analysis); print each signal's own
  letter beside its value (the scores already exist — the
  composite is their worst, and showing them makes every letter
  self-explaining). Lands while calibrate still exists, so the
  two grades can be sanity-checked against each other
  - **reports, never warns** (decided 2026-07-28): the report's
    job is a histogram faithful to what was measured, and a
    run's steadiness is largely the workload's character — a
    blocking round-trip is genuinely less steady than a
    spinning one. The letter is that fact, not a fault
- [[72]] 0.23.0-4 `feat: environment grade across the run`
  (done) — the box's own grade, with its own signals and
  letter, printed beside the run grade. Micro-probes time
  timer pairs and never touch the bench, so no workload
  character enters the letter; this is the environment
  certificate that must exist before -6 deletes `calibrate`
  (build-then-demolish)
  - retitled from "from warmup": a warmup-only window is
    ~17 ms against the run's seconds, and graded A on a 3900X
    that was demonstrably moving. Probes now also run at every
    batch seam — a seam already costs 1-2 ms, so a ~256 us
    probe is a fraction of a gap that exists anyway — and the
    series shares the batch series' time axis, which lets
    movement be *attributed*: a step in both at one instant is
    the machine, a step in only the run is the workload
  - `--no-env-probe` limits probing to warmup; default is on,
    the seam bias measured at +0.86% on a spinning 2t bench
    and ~0 on 1t
  - coordinate with the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo, which
    rewrites the same phase and now inherits this series as
    its convergence input; warnings stay off for now but this
    grade — a verdict on the box, not the bench — is the one
    that could earn them [[71]]
- [[73]] 0.23.0-5 `feat: split warmup and run environment
  stretches` (done)
  - promoted out of -7's precondition
  list to its own rung: the qualification selftest's observable *is*
  the environment grade, so restructuring it first means
  building that selftest once instead of twice

content.text:
Reacquainted: on `qymovnlztlkp` (empty `@`), last landed work commit is `qxlxtnouqwus feat: qualify-environment subcommand` = ladder rung 0.23.0-6, so the cycle sits at **-6 done, -7 next** (drop overhead calibration) then the bare `0.23.0` close-out. TODO.md line 96 still marks -6 `(current)`, which is stale as of that push.

## On the em-dash

Two different dashes are in play, and only one is the problem.

- **Structural dash** — glues a rung's *title* to its *body* on one line: `` - [[70]] 0.23.0-3 `feat: batch-based run gauge` (done) — relocate the -6 grade machinery… ``. That's a header and a paragraph pretending to be one bullet. This is the one to kill.
- **Rhetorical dash** — mid-sentence apposition inside otherwise fine prose: "a seam already costs 1-2 ms — a ~256 us probe is a fraction of a gap that exists anyway". Nothing wrong with it; AGENTS.md itself uses it ~111 times. Leave alone.

The structural sites in the 0.23.0 ladder are lines 29, 34, 38, 53, 97, 120 (and 136, see below). Rungs -5 (line 75) is already in the target shape, which is exactly why the inconsistency reads so loudly — half the ladder has a bare title line and half doesn't.

### Why the sub-bullet form is the right target

It isn't just taste; the AGENTS.md ladder template already implies it — `<title>` on its own line, then `- <item>` detail. The em-dash form is a violation that predates anyone noticing. And it has a concrete cost: rungs -3 and -4 currently have a dash-attached paragraph *plus* nested sub-bullets, so their detail lives at two indent levels for no semantic reason. Converting flattens them into one level of siblings — same shape as -5 — and the flattening is correct, since those paragraphs and those sub-bullets are all just "details of this rung".

It also makes the rung line scannable: `- [[70]] 0.23.0-3 \`feat: …\` (done)` is a fixed-width, greppable ladder row. Today you have to eye-parse where the title ends.

### Edge cases worth deciding before a sweep

- **Short tails.** Line 136: `` - [[N]] 0.23.0 `feat: grade the run from raw batches` — close-out and validation ``. Three words. A sub-bullet here is more scaffolding than content. My call: exempt a tail that fits on the title line and is a *label*, not a body — but honestly the close-out rung would read fine as the bare title with `close-out and validation` dropped entirely, since the bare `X.Y.Z` already means close-out.
- **Term–gloss one-liners.** `- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location…` (AGENTS.md, Memory section). That's a definition list, and the dash is doing the job a definition list does. Exempt. Proposed line: if the detail runs past ~one line, it's a body and wants a sub-bullet; a one-line gloss on a bolded term keeps its dash.
- **`## Todo` entries.** Same pattern, e.g. line 153 `1. Dynamic startup warmup — replace the fixed \`WARMUP = 10_000\`…`. Converting these is *more* valuable than the ladder, because AGENTS.md says a Todo is referred to durably by its title — a bare title line makes that mention unambiguous to grep instead of buried mid-sentence.

### Scope I'd propose

- **Now:** TODO.md — the 0.23.0 ladder plus the `## Todo` entries (lines 153, 245, 267 and their kin). One notes-only commit.
- **Also now, and cheaply:** codify it in AGENTS.md > Prose form as a sibling of *Semicolons inside bullets*. The two rules are the same idea: a bullet that hides structure inside running punctuation should expose the structure. Something like "Em dash between a bullet's title and its body" — a bullet whose dash separates a heading from a multi-line body is a title-and-body pretending to be one line; break the body into sub-bullets. Rhetorical and term-gloss dashes are unaffected.
- **Not now:** `notes/done.md`, `chores-01..03` — append-mostly history, same reasoning as AGENTS.md's "pre-existing sections keep their free-form text". `chores-04.md` is the live cycle file, so its section intros are fair game, but I'd check whether it actually has structural dashes before committing to it (its 134 dashes are likely mostly rhetorical).
- **Question for you:** should this ride as its own `docs:` rung inside 0.23.0, or wait and land as part of the close-out's notes tidy? A convention change touching AGENTS.md feels like it deserves its own commit rather than being buried in close-out.

**The plain version:** you've got two kinds of dash in the notes. One is normal English punctuation in the middle of a sentence and should stay. The other is being used as a colon — "here's the name of the thing, dash, now here's a paragraph about it" — and that one should become a bullet underneath instead. I'd fix TODO.md's ladder and its Todo list, write the rule down in AGENTS.md so it doesn't drift back, and leave the old finished notes files alone.

content.text:
Here's a concrete proposal — drop-in text, so you can diff it against vc-x1's version rather than reconcile two summaries.

**Placement:** `AGENTS.md` > `## Prose form`, as a new `###` immediately after *Semicolons inside bullets*. Same section, same shape, and the two rules are siblings in spirit.

**Heading:** `### Em dashes inside bullets` — chosen to parallel *Semicolons inside bullets* exactly (anchor `#em-dashes-inside-bullets`). If vc-x1 proposed something like "Em dash between title and body", the parallel with the semicolon rule is the tiebreaker I'd argue for.

---

```markdown
### Em dashes inside bullets

A bullet whose em dash separates a title from a body — `- Foo —
<paragraph about foo>` — is a heading and its detail pretending
to be one line. Break the body out into sub-bullets so the title
stands alone and the detail sits where detail goes.

- **Convert** when the dash's right-hand side is a *body*: more
  than about one line, or more than one sentence, or itself
  followed by sub-bullets (which strands the detail across two
  indent levels for no reason).
- **Leave** the em dash used as ordinary prose punctuation —
  apposition or aside inside a sentence ("a seam already costs
  1-2 ms — a fraction of a gap that exists anyway"). This rule
  is about structure, not the character.
- **Leave** a one-line term-gloss, where the bullet is an entry
  in a definition list: `- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root,
  committed, reviewable`. The dash is doing what a definition
  list does, and a sub-bullet for one line is more scaffolding
  than content.
- **Leave** a short tail that fits on the title line and names
  rather than explains (e.g. a close-out rung's `— close-out
  and validation`).

Not absolute: the line between a long gloss and a short body is
a judgment call, and one over-long dash is not worth a reflow on
its own. Applies to the surfaces Prose form covers, most visibly
ladder steps in `## In Progress`, `## Todo` entries, and chores
bullets. Pre-existing text in append-mostly files (`done.md`,
closed `chores-NN.md`) keeps its form; the rule applies going
forward.

**Why:** the same reason as [Semicolons inside
bullets](#semicolons-inside-bullets) — punctuation that hides
structure inside running text should give way to the structure.
A bare title line is also fixed-shape and greppable, which
matters wherever the title is the durable handle: a `## Todo`
entry is referred to by title, and a ladder step's title is
verbatim identical to its chores `##` header and its commit
title.
```

---

Three choices in there that I'd expect to be the actual points of disagreement with vc-x1, flagged so you can arbitrate:

- **The gloss exemption.** Without it the rule eats AGENTS.md's own definition-list bullets (the Memory section, the "Bullet *content* differs by surface" list), which are fine as they are. A stricter version that converts those too would churn a lot of good text.
- **The "not absolute" hedge.** Copied deliberately from the semicolon rule so the two read as a matched pair. A version without it is enforceable by a future `validate-repo` check; a version with it isn't. If vc-x1 is thinking about mechanical validation, that's a real argument for dropping the hedge and tightening "about one line" into a hard test (e.g. *the dash's right side wraps to a second source line*).
- **Framing as structure, not the character.** I'd resist any version phrased as "avoid em dashes" — the rhetorical dash is load-bearing in this project's prose and a blanket rule would strip it.

The intro of the proposed section uses a rhetorical dash pair itself, which is intentional: the rule demonstrates its own exemption in its first sentence.

content.text:
It simplifies it a lot — the ban subsumes the structural rule, because there's no longer a rhetorical/gloss distinction to draw. Everything I wrote as exemptions existed only to protect legitimate em dash uses; with none legitimate, the whole apparatus goes.

The residue is one sentence: banning the character doesn't by itself say *sub-bullets* — you could satisfy a ban by writing `- Foo: <paragraph>`. So the title/body case still needs naming.

Combined, that's one short `###` under Prose form, replacing my earlier proposal entirely:

```markdown
### No em dashes

Don't use `—`. At terminal sizes it reads like `-` or `--`, and
it can't be typed into a grep. Use a comma, parentheses, or two
sentences. Where an em dash was separating a bullet's title from
its body, that's a heading and a paragraph sharing a line: make
the body sub-bullets.
```

Six lines, and it's a net *shrink* if it also lets the *Semicolons inside bullets* rule stay as-is rather than gaining a sibling.

Two things to settle:

- **Sweep or going-forward?** There are ~350 existing sites (AGENTS.md 111, cycle-protocol 96, chores-04 134, TODO.md ~30). Going-forward-only means the rule's own documents visibly violate it for a long time, which reads as dead-letter. But each site needs a chosen replacement, so it's not a `sed`. My suggestion: sweep AGENTS.md + cycle-protocol + TODO.md (the live, frequently-read files) as one `docs:` rung, and let `done.md` / closed chores keep their text under the usual append-mostly exemption.
- **Don't allow `-` as the replacement.** Substituting ` - ` reintroduces exactly the visual collision you're objecting to, and inside a bullet it looks like a nested list marker. Worth the half-line in the rule if you think it'd be reached for; I left it out to stay short.

The plain version: since you're banning the character outright, all the careful "this dash is fine, that one isn't" text becomes unnecessary. The rule shrinks to "don't use it, and if you were using it to introduce a paragraph, that paragraph should have been a sub-bullet."

Reviewed `/home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/AGENTS.md` (uncommitted, in `uykyvknz`). The other three modified files belong to the stateless-push cycle, not this rule — only 4 added lines across `cycle-protocol.md` carry dashes, so no sweep happened.

## Better than my proposal — adopt

- **`–` too.** I missed the en dash. Right call.
- **"An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was not made."** That's the real insight, and it turns a typographic ban into three named repairs (sub-bullets / colon / comma-or-cut) instead of my one. Keep this framing verbatim.
- **Colon for term-definition.** Strictly better than my "exempt the one-line gloss" — it's consistent with an absolute ban *and* preserves the one-line-per-entry shape I was trying to protect.
- **Code span is a specimen, not a use**, aligned to the existing `[N]`-in-backticks precedent. Good reuse of vocabulary already in the file.
- **Scope inherited from Speculation marker**, and the cross-link added in the Prose form intro (with that intro's own dash converted). Both good.
- **Explicitly absolute, contrasted with the semicolon rule's "not absolute."** Necessary, since a hedge would make it uncheckable.

## What I'd cut

At ~30 lines it's now the longest subsection in Prose form, longer than the rule it parallels, in a file you're trying to shrink. Three cuts:

- **The asymmetric-cost paragraph** ("free to emit and paid on every read, so it accumulates without anyone having chosen it"). True, but it's rationale for a rule nobody will contest once stated. Two concrete reasons is enough.
- **"`…` and `→` carry no such ambiguity and are fine."** Scope creep, and internally inconsistent: `→` can't be typed at a terminal either, which is the disqualifier the sentence just invoked two lines earlier. Either drop it or the grep argument needs a caveat.
- **"checkable by byte scan, with code spans skipped."** Implementation guidance for a `validate-repo` check that doesn't exist. Belongs in a TODO entry.

## The one real inconsistency

`AGENTS.md` still has **113 lines containing `—`**, including line 7, six lines above the first heading. Combined with "this one is absolute" and "checkable by byte scan", that's a rule book violating its own absolute rule 113 times and claiming a checker that could never be switched on. "Applies going forward; existing text converts when touched" is a coherent policy, but not for an absolute rule in the document that declares it.

I'd sweep `AGENTS.md` and `notes/cycle-protocol.md` as part of the same commit — they're the read-most files and the ones that model the conventions — and let `done.md` / closed chores files keep their text. If a sweep isn't wanted now, drop "checkable by byte scan" until one lands.

## Merged text I'd propose we both adopt

```markdown
### No em dashes

Don't use `—` or `–` in durable text. Next to option syntax the
eye reads one as another flag, and neither can be typed at a
terminal, so both are invisible to ad-hoc grep. Unlike the
semicolon rule above, this one is absolute.

An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was
not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker).
A `—` inside a code span is a specimen, not a use.
```

19 lines instead of 30, and everything cut is either rationale, scope creep, or tooling notes.

**One open question for you to settle across both of us:** their scope is durable text only, so conversational replies still permit em dashes. But "reads like a flag in a terminal" is *most* true of conversation, which is where you actually read them at terminal width. I'd extend the rule to conversational output too — but that's a change to your reading experience, so it's your call, not a convention detail.

file.content:
## Prose form

Long-lived prose on this project follows one basic shape: a short intro
that explains the *why* or the high-level *what*, then a `-` bullet
list for the details. Wrap lines at ≤72 cols (bullet continuations
indent two spaces). Avoid wall-of-prose paragraphs — they hide the
structure that bullets make scannable.

Surfaces that use this shape:

- Module / function / struct / field doc comments in `.rs` files —
  see [Doc comments](#doc-comments-on-every-file-function-and-method).
- Commit message bodies (both work-repo and bot-repo). The
  ≤50-col title is the commit-specific add-on; see
  [Per-commit flow](notes/cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow).
- Chore descriptions in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` — see
  [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- Todo and Done entries in `TODO.md` when an entry needs more
  than one line of detail. Pure one-liners are still fine.

Bullet *content* differs by surface:

- **Commit bodies** — bullets are file-by-file: one bullet per file
  changed, file plus a one-line gist (e.g.
  `README.md: new Overview intro`). Source of truth for the
  mechanical edit list. The **version-of-record bump leads the
  list** — the manifest bullet (e.g. `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`)
  goes first, where a reader confirming which commit a version
  came from finds it at a glance instead of scanning to the
  bottom.
- **Chores / todo / done** — bullets are conceptual (design points,
  structural notes, the "what landed and why" at a notch above
  file-list granularity). Never a copy of the commit's edit list —
  see [Chores section content](#chores-section-content--no-edit-list-git-is-the-record).
- **Doc comments** — bullets are whatever structure fits (fields,
  cases, invariants).

### Problem + plan shape

`## In Progress` cycle blocks, chores section intros, and `## Todo`
entries use a sharper form of the same shape:

- **Problem statement** (the why) — one or two sentences;
  don't pad with intent, don't restate the plan.
- **Plan bullets** (the what/when) — formality differs by
  surface:
  - In Progress / chores: a committed ladder, one step per
    commit — see
    [Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
    for the per-step title + `(current)` / `(done)` form.
  - Todo entries: rough informal bullets, no numbering;
    formalized only when the entry is picked up into a
    cycle.

### Semicolons inside bullets

A bullet that joins multiple clauses with semicolons (`A; B; C`)
is a list hiding inside running prose — break the clauses into
sub-bullets so the structure shows. Semicolons in running prose
(intro paragraphs, sentence-joins) are fine. Not absolute: very
short clauses or tight pairs can stay joined inside a bullet when
breaking would be more noise than signal.

### Conventional-commit shape (ladder / chores / commit)

content.text:
Read the diff. No changes made here.

## What's better and I'd adopt

- **The rename to `### Typeable punctuation only`.** This is the right frame, and it fixes the inconsistency I flagged last round from the other direction. I said "cut the `…`/`→` sentence"; banning them instead is the better resolution, because the grep-and-terminal argument applies to them identically. The section title now states the principle rather than one instance of it.
- **`…` becomes `...`, `→` becomes `->`, the dashes have no single replacement.** That asymmetry paragraph is the most useful thing in the section. It explains why two of the four can be swept mechanically and two can't, which is exactly what a reader needs to know before touching old text.
- **"they cost nothing to write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates them."** I argued for cutting this. I'll concede: compressed to one clause it earns its place, because the sibling rule directly above is explicitly *not* absolute, so a reader legitimately asks why this one is.
- **"which is how this section names them"** — neat, and it preempts the obvious "your rule violates itself" objection.

## Pushback

**1. The sweep is half-done, and the half left undone is the one the section is mostly about.**

`AGENTS.md` now has 2 lines with `…`/`→`/`–` (the specimens in the rule itself) and **112 lines with `—`**. They swept the mechanical two and left the one that needs judgment. Worse, several untouched dashes sit on lines the diff *edited*:

```
-cargo cycle (fmt → clippy → test → install); skip-able for
+cargo cycle (fmt -> clippy -> test -> install); skip-able for
 notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. The full protocol
 — numbering, per-commit flow, reviewing changes, close-out,
```

Their own policy is "existing text converts when touched." That line was touched. So the document now bans four characters, uses one of them 112 times, and demonstrates skipping it on lines it was actively editing. I'd rather see the em dash sweep land in the same commit, or the rule ship without the absolute claim until it does. A rule that arrives already dead-letter teaches the opposite of what it says.

**2. The code-span exemption is written wider than they actually applied it.**

> A banned character inside a code span is a specimen, not a use

Read literally, that exempts *every* code span, which would have permitted leaving `` `.expect(…)` `` and `` `- …` `` alone. They converted those anyway, correctly. So the sentence and the practice disagree. The trailing clause gestures at the right rule but doesn't state it. I'd tighten to something like: *a banned character inside a code span is exempt only when the span is naming that character* — which is what "specimen" was reaching for, and it makes the byte-scan check implementable instead of ambiguous.

**3. The `// OK: …` heading rename has a repo-wide echo they didn't follow.**

Line 749 is now `### \`// OK: ...\` comments on \`unwrap*\` calls (Rust)`, but the convention is still spelled `// OK: …` in `notes/README.md:56`, `notes/chores/chores-04.md` (5 sites), and `notes/done.md:62`. No anchor link points at that heading, so nothing is broken — but the same convention now has two spellings, and the one in `README.md` is the discovery path. Also worth noting the anchor itself changed (`#-ok--comments-…` recomputes), so any future inbound link written against the old form silently misses.

**4. Comma splice** in "applies going forward, existing text converts when touched." Semicolon or period. Trivial, but it's in a section about punctuation.

## Where that leaves agreement

I'm fine adopting their section essentially as written, with two edits: the tightened code-span sentence from (2), and the comma fixed in (4). Everything else in it I'd take over what I currently have.

That means my `AGENTS.md` needs three changes to converge: rename `No em dashes` → `Typeable punctuation only`, add `…`/`→` plus the replacement paragraph, and update the cross-link in the Prose form intro. Say the word and I'll apply it.

The remaining genuine disagreement is (1): whether the em dash sweep lands with the rule or after it. My position is with it, at minimum for `AGENTS.md` and `cycle-protocol.md`.

input.old_string:
### No em dashes

Don't use `—` or `–` in durable text. Next to option syntax the
eye reads one as another flag, and neither can be typed at a
terminal, so both are invisible to ad-hoc grep. Unlike the
semicolon rule above, this one is absolute.

An em dash usually stands in for a structural decision that was
not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** takes a colon, which keeps a
  glossary or a command list at one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker).
A `—` inside a code span is a specimen, not a use.
input.new_string:
### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal.
Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a
compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the
semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to
write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no
single replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker);
applies going forward, existing text converts when touched. A
banned character inside a code span is exempt only when the
span is naming that character, which is how this section names
them; a `…` standing in for elided code is a use and converts.

Applied. My `### Typeable punctuation only` is now vc-x1's section with the two edits I pushed back on:

- **Code-span exemption tightened.** Theirs reads "a banned character inside a code span is a specimen, not a use", which literally exempts every code span and would have permitted leaving `` `.expect(…)` `` alone — which they converted anyway. Mine narrows it to *naming the character itself*, keeps the specimen/use vocabulary, and gives the `.expect` case as the worked example, since that's the one their own sweep decided.
- **Comma splice.** Split into two sentences rather than a second semicolon in the same breath as the scope link.

Everything else is verbatim theirs, including the sentence I'd argued for cutting last round.

Two open items, unchanged and not touched here:

- **My em dash sweep hasn't happened either.** This file still has 111 lines with `—`, plus 17 with `…`/`→`/`–` (lines 428, 457-458, 474, 600, 656-660, 721-755). So mine is now in the same position I criticized theirs for, one step further back — they at least swept the mechanical characters. If we agree the sweep lands with the rule, mine needs both halves; if it lands after, we should both drop "absolute" until then. Still my position that it should land together, at least for `AGENTS.md` and `notes/cycle-protocol.md`.
- **`// OK: …` naming echo.** Same issue exists here: the heading at line 724 and the sites at 721/727/734-755 all use `…`, and a rename changes that anchor. Worth doing as one piece with the sweep so the spelling never diverges across files, which is what happened on their side.

content.text:
`AGENTS-iiac-perf.md` is my `AGENTS.md` with exactly one addition: a nine-line quoted-text exemption at the end of *Typeable punctuation only*. Nothing else differs.

**Verdict: accept the idea, it closes a hole I opened.**

The hole is mine specifically. I tightened their code-span sentence to "a code span is exempt only when it is naming the character itself" — which, read straight, means a fenced block of pasted tool output or an error message gets converted. That's wrong, and their exemption is the fix. Their looser original wording accidentally covered this case; my tightening broke it. So the two edits belong together, and the exemption should sit right after the code-span sentence and say it overrides it, or a reader will apply the narrower rule and mangle a paste.

The commit-title argument is the strongest part and I wouldn't have thought of it: chores `##` headers are required to be *verbatim* identical to commit titles, so converting a historical title's em dash silently breaks both `git log --grep` and that identity rule. That's a real consequence of an innocuous-looking sweep, and it's worth the words.

**Two things I'd change:**

1. **"a pushed commit title" is ambiguous in the wrong direction.** A commit title is durable text the bot writes, so this must be a carve-out for *already-published* titles only. As written, someone can read it as licensing em dashes in commit titles generally, which would be the opposite of the rule. Needs an explicit "titles written from now on comply."
2. **The override isn't stated.** Per above, it needs to say it beats the code-span rule, otherwise the two paragraphs contradict each other for the common case of a quote inside backticks.

Proposed replacement for their paragraph:

```markdown
Text quoted from outside this repo's prose (tool output, an
error message, an already-published commit title) is
transcribed, not written, so it keeps its characters, and this
overrides the code-span rule above. It matters most for commit
titles: converting one stops it matching `git log --grep` and
breaks the verbatim identity that
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit)
requires between a commit title, its chores header, and its
`## Done` entry. Titles written from here on comply.
```

Same length, adds the override and the going-forward clause, and leads with the general principle ("transcribed, not written") rather than the instance — which also ties it cleanly to Speculation marker's scope, since that scope is text the bot *writes*.

Want me to apply that, or send it back to them first?

### Typeable punctuation only

Durable text uses punctuation that can be typed at a terminal.
Banned: `—`, `–`, `…`, `→`. None can be entered without a
compose key or a paste, so none can be grepped for, and an em
dash next to option syntax reads as another flag. Unlike the
semicolon rule above this one is absolute: they cost nothing to
write and are paid on every read, so a soft rule accumulates
them.

`…` becomes `...` and `→` becomes `->`. The dashes have no
single replacement, because an em dash usually stands in for a
structural decision that was not made. Make the decision:

- **A bullet's title and its body sharing a line** is a heading
  and a paragraph. Make the body sub-bullets.
- **A term and its definition** (`jj diff`, `<base>`, a flag)
  takes a colon, which keeps a glossary or a command list at
  one line per entry.
- **A prose aside** takes a comma, parentheses, or two
  sentences. Often the aside should just go.

Scope is the same as [Speculation marker](#speculation-marker).
It applies going forward; existing text converts when touched.
A code span is exempt only when it is naming the character
itself, which is how this section names them. A banned
character doing a job inside a code span is a use, not a
specimen, and converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes
`` `.expect(...)` ``.

Their tweak recasts the code-span sentence from "exempt only when…" to "not exempt in itself: specimen stays, use converts."

**Accept the framing.** Two real gains: it opens by correcting the misreading a reader actually makes (backticks look like an escape hatch), and it puts *specimen* and *use* adjacent, which is the section's own vocabulary and so reads as one contrast instead of two rules. One line shorter, too.

**Push back on the packaging.** The compression pours it all into a single sentence: colon, then a clause, then a `which`-relative, then a semicolon, then a `so`-clause. Four joins, no two naming the same relationship. That's precisely what this section's own intro calls out — "punctuation that joins clauses without naming their relationship is the same failure at sentence scale" — so it's a bad look three paragraphs later.

Same content, same line count, as sentences:

```markdown
converts when touched. A code span is not exempt by itself.
Naming the character is a specimen and stays, which is how this
section names them. A banned character doing a job is a use and
converts: `` `.expect(…)` `` becomes `` `.expect(...)` ``.
```

Also swaps "in itself" for "by itself", which reads less stilted and matches the following paragraph's "whether or not it sits in a code span".

732	default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
733	module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
734	inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
735	non-obvious WHY.
736	
737	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
738	`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
739	into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
740	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on
741	its own line in the rendered help.
742	
743	### `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
744	
745	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`,
746	`.expect(...)`, or the `.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings — prefer a shape
747	that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice patterns,
748	infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the
749	clearer code. This is a lean, not a ban: some sites are
750	legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
751	in scope:
752	
753	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)` — a panic path.
754	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` /
755	  `.unwrap_or_else(...)` — no panic, but a silently substituted
756	  value that can hide a wrong result.
757	
758	When one is used, three obligations attach:
759	
760	- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is
761	  acceptable:
762	  - `// OK: <specific reason>` — document the real
763	    precondition, invariant, or domain reason. Preferred
764	    whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
765	  - `// OK: obvious` — the default is self-evident from context
766	    (e.g. `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")` — empty desc ->
767	    empty title).
768	  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment).
769	    Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are not used because they require
770	    a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
771	- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so
772	  the site gets reviewed and appropriate uses are learned —
773	  don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
774	- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the
775	  site, because Rust projects enable the project-wide lints in
776	  `Cargo.toml`:
777	
778	  ```toml
779	  [lints.clippy]
780	  unwrap_used = "warn"
781	  expect_used = "warn"
782	  ```

**feat: grade the run from raw batches**

The 0.23.0 cycle, decided in
[Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run):
the overhead subtraction estimates an ill-defined quantity and
cancels in same-harness A/B anyway, while the calibration-time
grade certified the room, not the exam. Drop the adjustment
machinery; grade the run from its own time-ordered batches.

- [[67]] 0.23.0-0 `chore: open raw-batch grading cycle`
  (done)
- [[68]] 0.23.0-1 `feat: micro-probe inner-loop sizing`
  (done) —
  `pick_inner` inputs from a ~1 ms micro-probe (low quantile
  over back-to-back timer pairs), never printed; unhooks
  sizing from `cfg.overhead`
- [[69]] 0.23.0-2 `feat: time-ordered batch pipeline`
  (done) —
  samples land in a raw batch buffer; per-batch summaries
  (floor, mean, census counts) taken as batches fill, then
  bulk-record into the histogram; bounded memory
- [[70]] 0.23.0-3 `feat: batch-based run gauge` (done) — relocate
  the -6 grade machinery (signals, thresholds, letter) onto
  batch summaries: drift from floor movement, bursts localized
  in time, interference rate from census counts (absorbs the
  crossover entry's rate analysis); print each signal's own
  letter beside its value (the scores already exist — the
  composite is their worst, and showing them makes every letter
  self-explaining). Lands while calibrate still exists, so the
  two grades can be sanity-checked against each other
  - **reports, never warns** (decided 2026-07-28): the report's
    job is a histogram faithful to what was measured, and a
    run's steadiness is largely the workload's character — a
    blocking round-trip is genuinely less steady than a
    spinning one. The letter is that fact, not a fault
- [[72]] 0.23.0-4 `feat: environment grade across the run`
  (done) — the box's own grade, with its own signals and
  letter, printed beside the run grade. Micro-probes time
  timer pairs and never touch the bench, so no workload
  character enters the letter; this is the environment
  certificate that must exist before -6 deletes `calibrate`
  (build-then-demolish)
  - retitled from "from warmup": a warmup-only window is
    ~17 ms against the run's seconds, and graded A on a 3900X
    that was demonstrably moving. Probes now also run at every
    batch seam — a seam already costs 1-2 ms, so a ~256 us
    probe is a fraction of a gap that exists anyway — and the
    series shares the batch series' time axis, which lets
    movement be *attributed*: a step in both at one instant is
    the machine, a step in only the run is the workload
  - `--no-env-probe` limits probing to warmup; default is on,
    the seam bias measured at +0.86% on a spinning 2t bench
    and ~0 on 1t
  - coordinate with the "Dynamic startup warmup" Todo, which
    rewrites the same phase and now inherits this series as
    its convergence input; warnings stay off for now but this
    grade — a verdict on the box, not the bench — is the one
    that could earn them [[71]]
- [[73]] 0.23.0-5 `feat: split warmup and run environment
  stretches` (done)
  - promoted out of -7's precondition
  list to its own rung: the qualification selftest's observable *is*
  the environment grade, so restructuring it first means
  building that selftest once instead of twice
  - grade the probe series as two stretches — the warmup
    tail and the probes taken while the bench ran — rather
    than one blended series. `env warmup:` and `env run:`
    rows, composite is the worse of the two, so a reader sees
    which stretch earned the letter
  - warmup is scored on its **trailing 8 probes**, not the
    whole stretch: absorbing a ramp is what warmup is for, so
    the question is "did it end settled", not "was it steady
    throughout". This window is what the "Dynamic startup
    warmup" Todo turns into the exit condition
  - the failure being prevented is a fake step at the
    boundary: blended, a cold warmup followed by a hot run
    reads as a large step that nothing did wrong. Unit-tested
    both ways — the test asserts the blended series *would*
    have invented a >10% step [[71]]
- [[N]] 0.23.0-6 `feat: qualify-environment subcommand`
  (current) — `iiac-perf qualify-environment` respawns this binary
  `--runs` times at `--gap`, collects each run's environment
  grade, prints the table and a verdict, exits nonzero on
  FAIL. `tests/qualify_environment.rs` shrinks to invoking it and
  asserting on the exit status
  - the env knobs became real flags with real `--help`
    (`--runs`, `--gap`, `--print-only`, `-d` per child,
    `--pin` passed through), so the selftest is runnable by
    hand on any box — including one with no Rust toolchain,
    which is how the 7600x and the Dell get characterized
  - reads the environment grade, not the run grade: it is a
    test of the box. Both -5 stretches show — `env warmup` is
    the settling behaviour across respawns, `env run` whether
    it then held
  - verdict is grades, not values: median >= B and no run
    with `drift`/`step` at D/F in either stretch. Those two
    are the transition detectors; `spread`/`interference`
    wobble is ambient contamination and does not fail a run.
    The `mean` column is there because a two-state box is
    visible at a glance in it
  - FAILs on the 3900X today, correctly: that box shows the
    relaxation and the fix is the "Dynamic startup warmup"
    Todo, so a PASS would mean the test had stopped working
- [[N]] 0.23.0-7 `refactor: drop overhead calibration` —
  delete overhead.rs, the constants block, adjusted columns,
  the `calibrate` command; raw values only; one README
  sentence on apparatus framing. Deletion last: every
  capability has a living replacement before its old home
  goes (build-then-demolish, decided 2026-07-28)
  - what makes this safe on a cold box landed at -5.
    Calibration spins ~1 s on core 0 before any bench and the
    clock ramp measured at -4 takes ~150-200 ms, so
    calibration covers it five times over — an accidental
    pre-warm this rung removes. After deletion warmup sees the
    whole climb, which the split stretches absorb correctly
    [[71]]
  - re-check the -6 selftest's verdict thresholds against a
    genuinely cold first run once calibration is gone: its
    inputs move even though its observable does not
- [[N]] 0.23.0 `feat: grade the run from raw batches` —
  close-out and validation

## Todo

Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,

142	## Todo
143	
144	Entries are in **strict priority rank** — #1 highest,
145	descending. Reprioritize by moving an entry, then
146	`vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run TODO.md` to renumber.
147	The numbers are positional rank, not stable IDs — to refer
148	to a Todo, name it by its **title** (a greppable mention;
149	a numbered list item has no anchor to link to), not its
150	number. Long-tail entries
151	live in [todo-backlog.md](notes/todo-backlog.md). Use the
152	[Prose Form in AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#prose-form); deeper
153	detail goes in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` design
154	subsections (link via `[N]` ref).
155	
156	1. Dynamic startup warmup — replace the fixed
157	   `WARMUP = 10_000` step count in `harness.rs` with
158	   warm-until-stable: a fixed count's wall-clock scales with
159	   step cost, so the fastest benches warm ~10 us against
160	   frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of ms and
161	   `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
162	   [Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run);
163	   the retired -6 rung's design, revived for the run itself)
164	   - terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the
165	     0.22.0-4 "loop-only passes" sense) — a short, unrecorded,
166	     timed burst of bench steps yielding one floor. Not a
167	     "probe": `TProbe` is the measurement instrument, and the
168	     "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0 cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair
169	     frame measurement
170	   - fuse with `pick_inner` sizing: the warmup pass *is* the
171	     step-cost sizing pass, repeated back to back until K
172	     consecutive floors agree within tolerance; the final
173	     agreeing floor is the sizing input, so sizing is
174	     post-ramp by construction and convergence is tested on
175	     the number actually consumed (the micro-probe supplies
176	     the frame input, run after convergence)
177	   - K defaults to 3: two agreeing passes can certify a dwell
178	     at an intermediate P-state (the staircase ramp), not the
179	     top
180	   - **trailing-window grade = exit condition** (design,
181	     2026-07-28): rather than K agreeing floors, grade a
182	     *sliding window* over the -4 warmup probe series and warm
183	     until the trailing window reads A, or the cap. The exit
184	     condition and the warmup letter become one computation:
185	     exit on A means the run started post-ramp by
186	     construction, and hitting the cap reports whatever the
187	     window actually scored — the "run started unstable"
188	     signal, not a silent proceed. Window length takes the
189	     same "minimum count or minimum wall time, whichever is
190	     larger" shape as pass length (count because the split
191	     detector needs 4 points a side; wall time because the
192	     ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon). Signals: spread, drift,
193	     step — `interference` is the weak one [[71]]
194	   - **read the clock, not just the timing** (design,
195	     unmeasured): steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top"
196	     from "dwelling at an intermediate P-state", because a
197	     dwell *is* steady. Delivered frequency is an unprivileged
198	     sysfs read on both AMD boxes
199	     (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`) and the ramp is ~150-200 ms
200	     (measured at -4). Gate on **clock stability under load**,
201	     never on a fraction of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold
202	     would need tuning between 96.1% (3900X) and 99.7%
203	     (7600x) sustained, and a thermally-limited laptop
204	     plateaus lower still while that plateau is its honest
205	     clock. Optional by construction — `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
206	     amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
207	     reports requested rather than delivered — so read where
208	     present, fall back to timing-only. Report the ratio, do
209	     not grade on it [[71]]
210	   - report shape: normal output carries one warmup line
211	     (letter plus **settle time**, a number this project does
212	     not have yet and a real machine characteristic); `-v`
213	     shows the complete warmup picture, the per-probe table
214	     with the ramp's shape. The qualification selftest reading a
215	     table of settle times across respawns is a better
216	     observable than a table of blended letters
217	   - convergence is agreement, not direction — the 3900X is
218	     bistable (2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid
219	     repetition climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter,
220	     drift bracket caught 48.6 -> 45.3 mid-window, D/F),
221	     low-duty isolated runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and
222	     transitions straddle windows in *both* directions (the
223	     climb under quick cadence; the settle-back after load,
224	     which outlasted an 8 s gap once the box had been hot);
225	     fixed warmup absorbs only transitions shorter than
226	     itself, whatever their sign
227	   - floors, not means, so one preemption doesn't fake
228	     (in)stability; warm box exits near-immediately
229	   - slow steps (`inner` -> 1 territory): pass length adapts
230	     — minimum step count or minimum wall time, whichever is
231	     larger — so a floor is never one sample; the cap exit
232	     then distinguishes "floors disagreed" (unstable, gauge
233	     signal) from "too slow to certify K passes" (proceed,
234	     label the run uncertified — at `inner = 1` sizing can't
235	     be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes are
236	     low there)
237	   - hard cap at governor scale (a few hundred ms); hitting it
238	     unconverged is a gauge signal ("run started unstable"),
239	     not a silent proceed — and the cap doubles as the
240	     estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard entry (below)
241	     wants, so slow and non-converging benches share one
242	     diagnostic exit

1. Dynamic startup warmup — replace the fixed
   `WARMUP = 10_000` step count in `harness.rs` with
   warm-until-stable: a fixed count's wall-clock scales with
   step cost, so the fastest benches warm ~10 us against
   frequency-governor ramps of tens-to-hundreds of ms and
   `pick_inner` sizes mid-ramp (the 7600x F diagnosis,
   [Replanning II](notes/chores/chores-04.md#replanning-ii-drop-the-adjustment-grade-the-run);
   the retired -6 rung's design, revived for the run itself)
   - terminology: the warmup unit is a **warmup pass** (the
     0.22.0-4 "loop-only passes" sense) — a short, unrecorded,
     timed burst of bench steps yielding one floor. Not a
     "probe": `TProbe` is the measurement instrument, and the
     "micro-probe" is the 0.23.0 cycle's ~1 ms timer-pair
     frame measurement
   - fuse with `pick_inner` sizing: the warmup pass *is* the
     step-cost sizing pass, repeated back to back until K
     consecutive floors agree within tolerance; the final
     agreeing floor is the sizing input, so sizing is
     post-ramp by construction and convergence is tested on
     the number actually consumed (the micro-probe supplies
     the frame input, run after convergence)
   - K defaults to 3: two agreeing passes can certify a dwell
     at an intermediate P-state (the staircase ramp), not the
     top
   - **trailing-window grade = exit condition** (design,
     2026-07-28): rather than K agreeing floors, grade a
     *sliding window* over the -4 warmup probe series and warm
     until the trailing window reads A, or the cap. The exit
     condition and the warmup letter become one computation:
     exit on A means the run started post-ramp by
     construction, and hitting the cap reports whatever the
     window actually scored — the "run started unstable"
     signal, not a silent proceed. Window length takes the
     same "minimum count or minimum wall time, whichever is
     larger" shape as pass length (count because the split
     detector needs 4 points a side; wall time because the
     ramp is a ms-scale phenomenon). Signals: spread, drift,
     step — `interference` is the weak one [[71]]
   - **read the clock, not just the timing** (design,
     unmeasured): steadiness cannot tell "settled at the top"
     from "dwelling at an intermediate P-state", because a
     dwell *is* steady. Delivered frequency is an unprivileged
     sysfs read on both AMD boxes
     (`cpufreq/cpuinfo_avg_freq`) and the ramp is ~150-200 ms
     (measured at -4). Gate on **clock stability under load**,
     never on a fraction of `cpuinfo_max_freq`: a threshold
     would need tuning between 96.1% (3900X) and 99.7%
     (7600x) sustained, and a thermally-limited laptop
     plateaus lower still while that plateau is its honest
     clock. Optional by construction — `cpuinfo_avg_freq` is
     amd-pstate-specific and some drivers' `scaling_cur_freq`
     reports requested rather than delivered — so read where
     present, fall back to timing-only. Report the ratio, do
     not grade on it [[71]]

     not have yet and a real machine characteristic); `-v`
     shows the complete warmup picture, the per-probe table
     with the ramp's shape. The qualification selftest reading a
     table of settle times across respawns is a better
     observable than a table of blended letters

     bistable (2026-07-27 `calibrate` runs): sustained rapid
     repetition climbs it into a fast state (~0.445 ns/iter,
     drift bracket caught 48.6 -> 45.3 mid-window, D/F),
     low-duty isolated runs sit at ~0.489 (B), ~9% apart, and
     transitions straddle windows in *both* directions (the
     climb under quick cadence; the settle-back after load,
     which outlasted an 8 s gap once the box had been hot);
     fixed warmup absorbs only transitions shorter than
     itself, whatever their sign

     (in)stability; warm box exits near-immediately

     larger — so a floor is never one sample; the cap exit

     label the run uncertified — at `inner = 1` sizing can't
     be wrong and framing is negligible, so the stakes are

     unconverged is a gauge signal ("run started unstable"),

     estimate-phase deadline the `--pin` guard entry (below)

## Ideas

Longer-range thoughts, not yet ranked work. `-` bullets, no
numbering; promote into `## Todo` when one becomes actionable.

- Per-bench dependency isolation — motivated by dep provenance:
  the deps are the thing being measured, so a dep bump (e.g.
  iceoryx2 0.9.2 -> 0.9.3) legitimately moves that bench's
  numbers and shouldn't ride in silently. Options considered
  (2026-07-08):
  - Caveat first: a Cargo **workspace shares one Cargo.lock**
    across members — it scopes deps per package (ice benches
    alone pay for iceoryx2; faster `-p` builds; harness/probes
    become a library crate) but does *not* give per-bench lock
    isolation, and it splits the single CLI into many binaries.
  - Targeted updates (`cargo update -p <crate>`, never bare
    `cargo update`) — ~90% of the provenance benefit at zero
    structure cost; adoptable immediately as discipline.
  - Feature gates (`--features ice`) — solves build weight in
    the current single package, not lock isolation.
  - Truly standalone crates (own Cargo.lock each) — the only
    real per-bench dep isolation; maximum maintenance, and cuts
    against "same harness, same build" A/B comparability.
  - Current lean: targeted-update discipline now; feature gates
    or workspace only when bench families multiply.
- clap CompleteEnv dynamic completion (the `unstable-dynamic`
  feature): clap's native runtime completer (`COMPLETE=bash
  iiac-perf`) would give bash die-hards a compact column view
  without carapace; revisit if clap stabilizes it.
- Stability selftest mode (2026-07-27) — grade the
  environment more thoroughly than a single run's gauge: a
  product subcommand that respawns its own binary
  (`current_exe()`) N times at configurable cadences and
  reports cross-run gauge agreement ("is this box currently
  trustworthy for A/B?"). Precedent in-product: the
  calibration repeat self-check and `--blocks` both already
  validate by orchestrated repetition; this is the next ring
  out. Subsumes `tests/qualify_environment.rs`'s orchestration —
  the test reduces to asserting on the verdict, and its
  env-var knobs become clap flags. Concrete motivation
  (2026-07-27): the qualification test can't run on the 7600x,
  which has only the installed binary — environment
  qualification shouldn't require a source tree.
  **Promoted 2026-07-28**: the minimal version is the
  0.23.0-6 ladder rung (`qualify-environment subcommand`); what
  remains here for later is the fuller mode — cadence
  sweeps, richer cross-run reporting.
- Tick-phase avoidance (2026-07-27): the scheduler tick is
  periodic per-CPU (~300/s at CONFIG_HZ=300) and a tick hit is
  an unmistakable outlier, so predict the next tick from
  detected hits and pause measuring ~30 us around it — ~1%
  duty cost, no governor exposure with governor+EPP
  `performance`. Doesn't improve the bulk stats (tick hits
  are already detected and trimmed); buys a cleaner
  above-crossover tail on unmodified machines, so rarer
  aperiodic events (device IRQs, SMIs, code slow paths)
  become visible over the periodic contaminant. Check the
  interaction with dither (anti-phase scheduling must not
  introduce a systematic phase bias), and compare against
  `nohz_full`/`isolcpus` isolation — which abolishes the tick
  on a dedicated core and strictly dominates when a reboot is
  allowed — before building.

## Bugs

_See [bugs.md](notes/bugs.md)._

## Done

and older `## Done` sections are moved to [done.md](notes/done.md) to keep this file small.

1	# AGENTS.md - Bot Instructions
2	
3	## Project Structure
4	
5	This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:
6	
7	1. **Work repo** (`/` — project root): the project's generated
8	   artifact — code, prose, image, song, whatever it produces.
9	2. **Bot repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.
10	
11	Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.
12	
13	**Terminology.** "Work repo" and "bot repo" are the standard
14	names; write them as two words, adding a hyphen only when the
15	pair sits directly in front of another noun ("work-repo
16	commit", "bot-repo side"). Notes:
17	
18	- `.claude` is the bot repo's *path*, not its name — commands
19	  (`-R .claude`) and ochid paths (`/.claude/<chid>`) keep the
20	  literal path.
21	- The vc-x1 CLI's scope name for the work repo is `code`
22	  (`--scope=code|bot|code,bot`).
23	- "Work commit" / "Work-N" (capitalized) is a cycle-stage term
24	  (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol)), not a repo name; a
25	  generic commit landing in the work repo is a "work-repo
26	  commit", never a bare "work commit".
27	
28	**Committing vs pushing.** Default to `vc-x1 push` — it commits and
29	publishes both repos together, each carrying one `ochid:` pointing at
30	the other (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol) and
31	[ochid trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). Use a bare
32	`jj commit` (see [jj Basics](#jj-basics)) only when:
33	
34	- the change will never be published — no `ochid:`;
35	- the commit will be squashed away before its series is pushed

# AGENTS.md - Bot Instructions

## Project Structure

This project uses **two separate jj-git repos**:

1. **Work repo** (`/` — project root): the project's generated
   artifact — code, prose, image, song, whatever it produces.
2. **Bot repo** (`/.claude/`): Contains Claude Code session data.

Both repos are managed with `jj` (Jujutsu), which coexists with git.

**Terminology.** "Work repo" and "bot repo" are the standard
names; write them as two words, adding a hyphen only when the
pair sits directly in front of another noun ("work-repo
commit", "bot-repo side"). Notes:

- `.claude` is the bot repo's *path*, not its name — commands
  (`-R .claude`) and ochid paths (`/.claude/<chid>`) keep the
  literal path.
- The vc-x1 CLI's scope name for the work repo is `code`
  (`--scope=code|bot|code,bot`).
- "Work commit" / "Work-N" (capitalized) is a cycle-stage term
  (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol)), not a repo name; a
  generic commit landing in the work repo is a "work-repo
  commit", never a bare "work commit".

**Committing vs pushing.** Default to `vc-x1 push` — it commits and
publishes both repos together, each carrying one `ochid:` pointing at
the other (see [Cycle Protocol](#cycle-protocol) and
[ochid trailers](#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). Use a bare
`jj commit` (see [jj Basics](#jj-basics)) only when:

- the change will never be published — no `ochid:`;
- the commit will be squashed away before its series is pushed
  (loop-and-squash) — no `ochid:`; it disappears in the squash;
- the commit will be pushed later as a non-top commit — `jj commit`
  and add its `ochid:` now, because `vc-x1 push` stamps only the
  topmost commit it pushes, never the ancestors.

**What "commit" and "push" mean.** In an instruction, "commit",
"push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push` — land *and*
publish — unless stated otherwise. A bare `jj commit` is asked for
by name: "local commit", "save locally", "just `jj commit`" (the
cases above). So the spoken default is publish; the local-only
save is the named exception. The approval around a push —
interactive by default, waived only by an explicit scoped
delegation — is the cycle protocol's
[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Repo Paths (relative from project root)

- Work repo: `.` (project root)
- Bot repo: `.claude`
  (symlink from `~/.claude/projects/<path-to-project-root>/.claude`)

## Working Directory

Prefer staying in the project root. Use `-R` flags or absolute paths
to target other directories rather than `cd`. If `cd` seems necessary,
discuss with the user first — losing track of cwd causes subtle
command failures downstream.

When invoking shell commands, prefer the shortest unambiguous path —
usually relative to cwd (`ls notes/`, not
`ls /home/wink/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/notes/`). Long absolute paths
clutter the transcript without adding information. Out-of-workspace
paths (`/tmp/...`, `~/.config/...`) stay absolute. Read/Edit/Write
tool args also stay absolute — that's a tool-boundary constraint,
not a stylistic choice.

Run **one command per shell invocation** — don't bundle several
steps into a single compound script (`a && b; c`). Bundling hides
which step produced which output and makes a failure ambiguous;
executing one at a time keeps the details visible and reviewable.
Exceptions are a genuine pipeline (`grep | sort`) or a tight,
inseparable pair where the join is the point.

## File reads — read the slice you need

Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the
slice your task needs; grep or read further on demand.

- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read) — first
  ~60 lines covers intro + `## In Progress` + the top of the
  ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`; read
  further only when chasing a lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a
  `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`** — the long-tail backlog
  (lower-priority entries below the ranked `## Todo`). Read
  only when picking up a backlog item; grep to locate it
  first.
- **`notes/bugs.md`** — the bug list. Small; read whole
  when triaging a bug or chasing the `## Bugs` pointer in
  TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`** —
  historical / append-mostly. Scan headings first
  (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only
  the section you need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md`
grows every cycle, so the backlog and bugs live in files
under `notes/` rather than inline; the same "slice you
need" rule applies to historical files.

## Memory

Do not use the bot's per-project memory directory
(`~/.claude/projects/<path>/memory/`). In a dual-repo setup with
AGENTS.md it provides no capability AGENTS.md doesn't already cover,
and it loses on discoverability:

- **AGENTS.md** — at the repo root, a well-known location for bot
  instructions, committed, reviewable, visible to every collaborator
  (human or bot).
- **Memory directory** — hidden under the user's home, tied to one
  machine, invisible to anyone but the bot, never diffed or reviewed.

Easy for everyone to find beats convenient for the bot alone. Put

135	
136	When a conversational reply centers on a technical explanation
137	(measurement theory, statistics, hardware behavior), end it
138	with a short plain-language synopsis — no jargon, no symbols —
139	so the reader can check their understanding against the
140	technical version.
141	
142	**Why:** the technical form is precise but easy to misread;
143	the plain form catches misunderstandings early, when they are

147	entry should already lead with the why). Mark it clearly (e.g.
148	"The plain version:"). A reply that is already plain needs no

152	
153	Durable text the bot writes — AGENTS.md, `notes/`, commit bodies,
154	chores sections — should stick to observations and direct descriptions
155	of the code or data. If a mechanism, hypothesis, or causal claim
156	enters the text, prefix it with "We think ..." (a royal "we") so a
157	reader can tell the measured from the inferred.
158	
159	**Why:** unmarked speculation reads like evidence, and a future reader
160	(or the bot on a later session) can pick it up as a known fact when
161	it's not. Measured / inferred is a distinction worth keeping visible
162	in the written record.
163

165	marker. Prefix with "We think ..." (or a close variant like
166	"Our guess is ...") when the claim is a mechanism ("X wins
167	because Y caches better"), a cause ("the drift was due to thermal
168	state"), a prediction ("this should scale linearly"), or any

174	diff, commit, push, history rewrite). jj coexists with the git
175	backend, so the repo *can* be driven with raw `git`, but this
176	project's workflow — bookmarks, the working-copy `@` model, ochid
177	trailers — is expressed in jj terms; reaching for `git` invites
178	state that doesn't match the jj documentation here. There is no
179	`jj mv`: to move/rename a tracked file, just `mv` it on disk and
180	jj detects the rename by content.
181	
182	- `jj st -R .` / `jj st -R .claude` — show working copy status
183	- `jj log -R .` / `jj log -R .claude` — show commit log
184	- `jj commit -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — finalize working copy into a commit
185	- `jj describe -m "title" -m "body" -R <repo>` — set description without committing
186	- `jj git push --bookmark <name> -R <repo>` — push a bookmark (no
187	  `--allow-new` flag; jj pushes new bookmarks without special flags)
188	- In jj, the working copy (@) is always a mutable commit being edited.
189	  `jj commit` finalizes it and creates a new empty working copy on top.
190	- The bot repo always has uncommitted changes during an active
191	  session because session data updates continuously.
192	- `jj rebase` uses `--onto`/`-o` to name the destination(s).

198	counterpart in the other repo, so the "what" (code) and the
