640	
641	`Commits:` uses the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
642	[Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)),
643	**double-bracketed** so the brackets render — `Commits: [[3]]`,
644	or `Commits: [[3]],[[5]]` for several. (`[[3]]` shows as a
645	literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner
646	`[3]` resolves against its `[3]:` definition — CommonMark /
647	GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The `# References` definition
648	puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
649	40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
650	
651	```
652	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
653	```
654	
655	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short; GitHub /
656	  GitLab resolve a unique prefix to the canonical commit page
657	  (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
658	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous —
659	  it survives a repo host change, `git show <40-hex>` works in
660	  any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a
661	  database, say) gets the canonical identifier.
662	
663	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a
664	**permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived release/patch
665	branch) — a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way. A commit
666	can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later:
667	every section opens with an **empty `Commits:`**, and each push
668	backfills the `Commits:` of the commits the previous push made
669	permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
670	lands. The commit itself is the record, and
671	`git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
672	[Commits backfill](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
673	
674	## Cycle Protocol
675	
676	Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`) ->
677	Work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare
678	`X.Y.Z`). Each commit runs through a per-commit flow whose
679	validation step is medium-specific — the Rust example is the
680	cargo cycle (fmt -> clippy -> test -> install); skip-able for
681	notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. The full protocol
682	— numbering, per-commit flow, reviewing changes, close-out,
683	pushing, ochid trailers, sub-cycles — lives in
684	[`notes/cycle-protocol.md`](notes/cycle-protocol.md). Read
685	it before any commit work — and before any push, cycle or
686	not: pushes always need per-push user approval (see
687	[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy)).
688	
689	**Versioning.** How this repo numbers cycles, where the
690	version-of-record lives, and its bump cadence are
691	project-specific and documented in
692	[versioning.md](notes/versioning.md) — the single source of
693	truth that AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md refer to
694	abstractly.
695	
696	**Hard stop after push/squash-push.** Once a push or bot-repo
697	squash-push is invoked (`vc-x1 push` does both), do no further
698	work — no verification, no summary, no next-step offers —
699	until the user speaks. Put all closing words *before* the
700	invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
701	visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
702	acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed") — never a summary or more
703	work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's
704	direction. See
705	[After push or squash-push](notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).
706	
707	**`vc-x1 push` behaviors to keep in mind.** Two, independent
708	of project language:
709	
710	- **Preflight** checks repo state only — bookmark tracking,
711	  the bot-published invariant (`main == main@origin` in the
712	  bot repo), and a `sync --check`. It runs no build or
713	  tests: vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents
714	  beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`. The medium's
715	  validation (e.g. the Rust cargo cycle) is the per-commit
716	  flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`.
717	- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself —
718	  don't hand-write them into the commit body or
719	  `--title`/`--body`.
720	
721	
722	## Code Conventions
723	
724	### Doc comments on every file, function, and method
725	
726	Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
727	function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
728	one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
729	comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
730	[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).
731	
732	This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
733	default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
734	module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
735	inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
736	non-obvious WHY.
737	
738	**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
739	`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
740	into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
741	any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on
742	its own line in the rendered help.
743	
744	### `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)
745	
746	The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`,
747	`.expect(...)`, or the `.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings — prefer a shape
748	that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice patterns,
749	infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the
750	clearer code. This is a lean, not a ban: some sites are
751	legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
752	in scope:
753	
754	- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)` — a panic path.
755	- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` /
756	  `.unwrap_or_else(...)` — no panic, but a silently substituted
757	  value that can hide a wrong result.
758	
759	When one is used, three obligations attach:

permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
lands. The commit itself is the record, and
`git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See cycle-protocol
[Commits backfill](notes/cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).

## Cycle Protocol

Every change runs as a **cycle**: Preparation (`X.Y.Z-0`) ->
Work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) -> Close-out (bare
`X.Y.Z`). Each commit runs through a per-commit flow whose
validation step is medium-specific — the Rust example is the
cargo cycle (fmt -> clippy -> test -> install); skip-able for
notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out. The full protocol
— numbering, per-commit flow, reviewing changes, close-out,
pushing, ochid trailers, sub-cycles — lives in
[`notes/cycle-protocol.md`](notes/cycle-protocol.md). Read
it before any commit work — and before any push, cycle or
not: pushes always need per-push user approval (see
[Pushing policy](notes/cycle-protocol.md#policy)).

**Versioning.** How this repo numbers cycles, where the
version-of-record lives, and its bump cadence are
project-specific and documented in
[versioning.md](notes/versioning.md) — the single source of
truth that AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md refer to
abstractly.

**Hard stop after push/squash-push.** Once a push or bot-repo
squash-push is invoked (`vc-x1 push` does both), do no further
work — no verification, no summary, no next-step offers —
until the user speaks. Put all closing words *before* the
invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed") — never a summary or more
work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's
direction. See
[After push or squash-push](notes/cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

**`vc-x1 push` behaviors to keep in mind.** Two, independent
of project language:

- **Preflight** checks repo state only — bookmark tracking,
  the bot-published invariant (`main == main@origin` in the
  bot repo), and a `sync --check`. It runs no build or
  tests: vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents
  beyond `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`. The medium's
  validation (e.g. the Rust cargo cycle) is the per-commit
  flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself —
  don't hand-write them into the commit body or
  `--title`/`--body`.


## Code Conventions

### Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every
function and method must have a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief —
one sentence of purpose is often enough; the discipline is that the
comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments"
default that applies to inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the
module / item surface are expected; inline explanatory comments
inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive
`--help` output. Clap reflows by default and collapses bullets
into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on
its own line in the rendered help.

### `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`,
`.expect(...)`, or the `.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings — prefer a shape
that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice patterns,
infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the
clearer code. This is a lean, not a ban: some sites are
legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)` — a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` /
  `.unwrap_or_else(...)` — no panic, but a silently substituted
  value that can hide a wrong result.

# Cycle protocol

This protocol uses [Prose form](../AGENTS.md#prose-form). It
contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.

The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
the conversation — code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning); substitute your medium's
equivalents — this project's manifest is recorded in
[versioning.md](versioning.md).

## Cycles

A cycle has three phases:

- **[Preparation](#preparation)** (`X.Y.Z-0`) — the cycle's
  first commit, when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits
  it and starts at `-1` — see
  [versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)). Sets up the
  cycle:
  - Bump the version-of-record to `X.Y.Z-0` (where it lives
    and the suffix scheme are project-specific — see
    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked,
    #1) into `## In Progress` (bold title + succinct problem
    statement + plan ladder).
  - Open the [chores section](#chores-sections).
- **[Work-N](#work-n)** (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...) — the
  commits that implement the change. As many as the change
  needs; each runs through the
  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
- **[Close-out](#close-out)** (bare `X.Y.Z`) — the cycle's
  last commit. Bookkeeping only:
  - Move the picked-up item to a one-line entry in
    `## Done`.
  - Move the `## In Progress` block into the
    [chores section](#chores-sections).
  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
    changed.

A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
either incrementally or as one batch at close-out; the
result must always be published at close-out. See
[Pushing](#pushing).

**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
warrant its own ladder, it subdivides — `X.Y.Z-3.0`
Preparation, `X.Y.Z-3.1` / `X.Y.Z-3.2` Work, `X.Y.Z-3`
Close-out. The same three-phase shape applies recursively
at every depth. See [Numbering](#numbering) for the
suffix rule and [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)
for the local-ladder mechanics.

## Chores sections

A **chores section** is a `##` section in
`notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work. In
general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch
should have a reference to it on a `Commits:` list in a
chores file.

The phrase **"Open" the chores section** means append a
`##` header to the current `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`
with the title it records (e.g. `## refactor: foo bar`),
followed by an **empty `Commits:`** line. **Each work commit
then appends its own As-built rung + narrative note as it
lands** — the chores record is built up per commit, not held
back and written all at once at close-out; close-out only
*finalizes* (title sync, design subsections, retiring the
`## In Progress` block). The `Commits:` line is backfilled
later, once the commit is permanent (see
[Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).

Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync,
design subsection pattern, `Commits:` formatting) live in
AGENTS.md [Chores conventions](../AGENTS.md#chores-conventions).

### Commits backfill

A chores section's `Commits:` line cites the commit(s) it
records, by SHA — but a SHA isn't stable until the commit
lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
release/patch branch that won't be rewritten); a rebase or
squash rewrites it on the way. So:

- A chores section is **opened with an empty `Commits:`** line.
- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**,
  where its SHA is final. A commit can't record its own SHA
  (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one
  push later: **each push backfills the `Commits:` of the
  commits the previous push made permanent.** On a topic
  branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands —
  so no SHA is ever written that a later rebase could
  invalidate.

Use `[[N]]` refs — several as `[[N]],[[M]]` only when one
section records multiple commits (a merge non-ff close-out) —
with the commit URL + 40-hex SHA in the file's `# References`
(format in AGENTS.md
[Chores commit references](../AGENTS.md#chores-commit-references)).
A section's `##` title matches its commit title, so a rare
deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
`git log --grep "<title>"`.

The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma — a
**per-close-out** model (recording a cycle's SHAs at its
close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: a recorded
SHA must be permanent.

## Preparation

The cycle's first commit (`X.Y.Z-0`), when the cycle needs
setup (a lightweight cycle omits it — see
[versioning.md](versioning.md#step-numbering)):

- **Bump the version-of-record** to `X.Y.Z-0`. Where it
  lives, the suffix scheme, and any derived files (a
  lockfile, a sourced manifest version) are
  project-specific — see [versioning.md](versioning.md).

396	close-out commit, `<prev>` the previous cycle's close-out
397	(the current `main` tip), `<work-tip>` the cycle's last
398	Work commit:
399	
400	1. **Rebase the close-out into a merge** — `jj rebase -r
401	   <closeout> --onto <prev> --onto <work-tip>`.
402	   - `-r <closeout>` keeps the `<closeout>` commit in place.
403	   - `--onto <prev>` becomes its first parent (trunk).
404	   - `--onto <work-tip>` becomes the second parent.
405	
406	   Together these make `<closeout>` a merge of
407	   `<prev>` + `<work-tip>`, forming a trapezoidal commit.
408	2. **Use `jj new <merge>`** to add an empty `@` above the
409	   merge. The rebase left `@` *on* the now-content-bearing
410	   merge, which git/IDE diff views show as uncommitted;
411	   `jj new` restores the clean empty `@` on top.
412	3. **Push** — `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
413	
414	**Post-hoc caveat.** If the cycle was already pushed
415	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) its commits are
416	immutable: the rebase needs `--ignore-immutable` and the
417	push force-updates `main`.
418	The standard sequence assumes the merge is set up *before*
419	the close-out push.
420	
421	**Viewing the result (not a push step).** After merge
422	non-ff close-outs land, read the history with
423	`jj log -r ..@ -n <N>`: the graph renders each cycle as its
424	trapezoid — close-out titles down the trunk's left edge, the
425	cycle's Work rungs indented on the side leg — so trunk and
426	internals are both visible at once. For git-side tooling
427	(which lists commits flat instead of drawing the graph),
428	`git log --first-parent` recovers the trunk view — one
429	close-out merge per cycle, rungs skipped; plain `git log`
430	interleaves every cycle's rungs into one long list.
431	
432	### vc-x1 push wrapper
433	
434	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
435	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
436	work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
437	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
438	
439	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
440	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
441	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
442	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md` —
443	this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
444	
445	### .claude cadence
446	
447	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
448	with every work-repo commit in that push.
449	
450	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
451	across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
452	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
453	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
454	
455	`.claude` is a linear journal — all session work lives
456	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
457	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
458	work-repo branches** — risks the bot steering session
459	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
460	
461	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
462	session information created, which we don't worry about.
463	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
464	remain empty.
465	
466	### Bot communication at the reviews
467	
468	Use plain prose — no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
469	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
470	
471	- **At Work review** — summarize what changed and stop.
472	  "Work complete. Please review."
473	- **At Commit Description review** — present `$TITLE`
474	  and `$BODY` explicitly; ask permission to commit/push.
475	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
476	  --body ...` invocation by default.
477	- **At Post close-out review** — surface the shape
478	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target;
479	  wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
480	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
481	
482	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
483	
484	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
485	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper — whose last stage publishes
486	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
487	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
488	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
489	the next step seems obvious — wait.**
490	
491	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
492	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
493	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
494	  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
495	  turn's *final* push.
496	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal — everything after
497	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
498	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
499	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit; the final push's
500	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
501	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
502	  user, after the turn, can capture it
503	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
504	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
505	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
506	  visible token after the tool returns; if so, emit a bare
507	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed") — never a summary,
508	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
509	  closing line after the push — a known slip.
510	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
511	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
512	  quiet — it flushes all bot session information into the
513	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
514	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
515

(which lists commits flat instead of drawing the graph),

interleaves every cycle's rungs into one long list.

### vc-x1 push wrapper

`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
work-repo bookmark only; the bot repo is always pinned to
`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).

**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape; other
shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are

this protocol describes only the stable mechanism.

with every work-repo commit in that push.

The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
across the cycle; its change ID stays stable across
snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.

on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do

via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper — whose last stage publishes
the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
the next step seems obvious — wait.**

- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
  intermediate push just a step; the hard stop lands on the
  turn's *final* push.
- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal — everything after

516	### Recovery
517	
518	- **If push exits before its last stage** — `push-work`
519	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish didn't run
520	  (`squash-push-bot` in `vc-x1 push --status` / `--from`
521	  stage names) — run the squash+push by hand:
522	
523	  ```
524	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
525	  ```
526	
527	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
528	  exit — no log file to chase.
529	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
530	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
531	  agents).
532	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
533	    command runs — the invocation's own record plus any
534	    closing response land after the squash.
535	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
536	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
537	    change; it is not under the user's control.)
538	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
539	    `@` non-empty — e.g. the bot's back end may decide to
540	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
541	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
542	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
543	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
544	- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band
545	  recovery — `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push
546	  <bookmark> --restart` — otherwise push resumes from a
547	  stale stage.
548	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
549	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
550	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
551	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
552	  push.
553	- **`vc-x1 push` after a manual merge setup published an
554	  empty commit** (seen at the 0.22.0 close-out). `vc-x1
555	  push` *creates* the work commit itself from pending
556	  changes + `--title`/`--body`; it does not publish an
557	  already-committed shape. Invoked after the
558	  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) (work repo
559	  clean, merge in place), it minted an **empty** commit on
560	  the old `main` tip, stamped the ochid on it, and pushed
561	  that — leaving the merge unreferenced and `main` without
562	  the cycle's content. Prevention: after a manual shape
563	  setup, push with `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`
564	  directly (the recipe's step 3), never `vc-x1 push`.
565	  Recovery, in order (nothing is lost — the merge still
566	  exists):
567	  1. `jj describe <merge>` to append the
568	     `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>` trailer the stray got
569	     instead (rewrites the merge's commit id; its chid —
570	     what the bot side references — is stable).
571	  2. `jj abandon <stray> --ignore-immutable`.
572	  3. `jj bookmark set main -r <merge> --allow-backwards`,
573	     `jj new <merge>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main
574	     -R .` (remote rewrite — needs approval).
575	  4. Bot repo: `jj describe <bot-commit> --ignore-immutable
576	     -R .claude` to point its `ochid:` at the merge's chid,
577	     then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .claude`
578	     (restores the `main == main@origin` preflight
579	     invariant).
580	
581	  The recovered shape, `jj log -r ..@` (0.22.0, elided):
582	
583	  ```
584	  @  smpozlop … (empty) (no description set)
585	  ◆    yzvlvtku … main d9bb5882
586	  ├─╮  fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise
587	  │ ◆  ztxvxuru … fix-calibration f4b155a8
588	  │ │  feat: always-on calibration self-checks
589	  │ ~  (three more rungs)
590	  │ ◆  tskxkxsk … 6d5784de
591	  ├─╯  fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
592	  ◆  sktyvwrq … f006b09e
593	  │  feat: amortized + cached calibration

### Recovery

- **If push exits before its last stage** — `push-work`
  succeeded but the bot-repo publish didn't run
  (`squash-push-bot` in `vc-x1 push --status` / `--from`
  stage names) — run the squash+push by hand:

  ```
  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
  ```

  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
  exit — no log file to chase.
- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
  agents).
  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
    command runs — the invocation's own record plus any
    closing response land after the squash.
  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
    change; it is not under the user's control.)
  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
    `@` non-empty — e.g. the bot's back end may decide to
    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
- **Clear push's saved state** after any out-of-band
  recovery — `rm .vc-x1/push-state.toml` or `vc-x1 push
  <bookmark> --restart` — otherwise push resumes from a
  stale stage.
- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push; that is a
  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
  push.
- **`vc-x1 push` after a manual merge setup published an
  empty commit** (seen at the 0.22.0 close-out). `vc-x1
  push` *creates* the work commit itself from pending
  changes + `--title`/`--body`; it does not publish an
  already-committed shape. Invoked after the
  [Merge non-ff recipe](#merge-non-ff-recipe) (work repo
  clean, merge in place), it minted an **empty** commit on
  the old `main` tip, stamped the ochid on it, and pushed
  that — leaving the merge unreferenced and `main` without
  the cycle's content. Prevention: after a manual shape
  setup, push with `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`
  directly (the recipe's step 3), never `vc-x1 push`.
  Recovery, in order (nothing is lost — the merge still
  exists):
  1. `jj describe <merge>` to append the
     `ochid: /.claude/<bot-chid>` trailer the stray got
     instead (rewrites the merge's commit id; its chid —
     what the bot side references — is stable).
  2. `jj abandon <stray> --ignore-immutable`.
  3. `jj bookmark set main -r <merge> --allow-backwards`,
     `jj new <merge>`, then `jj git push --bookmark main
     -R .` (remote rewrite — needs approval).
  4. Bot repo: `jj describe <bot-commit> --ignore-immutable
     -R .claude` to point its `ochid:` at the merge's chid,
     then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .claude`
     (restores the `main == main@origin` preflight
     invariant).

  The recovered shape, `jj log -r ..@` (0.22.0, elided):

  ```
  @  smpozlop … (empty) (no description set)
  ◆    yzvlvtku … main d9bb5882
  ├─╮  fix: calibration robust to codegen and noise
  │ ◆  ztxvxuru … fix-calibration f4b155a8
  │ │  feat: always-on calibration self-checks
  │ ~  (three more rungs)
  │ ◆  tskxkxsk … 6d5784de
  ├─╯  fix: pair frame/call against a loop-only pass
  ◆  sktyvwrq … f006b09e
  │  feat: amortized + cached calibration
  ```

## Iterative work

When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
from incremental review, loop:

1. `jj new -R .` — fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
2. Make the next round of changes.
3. User reviews the round (see
   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
   new empty `@`.
5. If not done, go to step 2.

Same jj mechanics as a
[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
single-commit scope — the version
doesn't change.

## Sub-cycle ladders

When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
[Numbering](#numbering) for suffix nesting), its Work
commits typically live as a local jj `@` chain and
**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch —
for review and bisection only.

### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder

For each Work commit in the ladder:

1. `jj new -R .` — create a fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
   --bins`). **Non-negotiable** — for code, build and clippy
   alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the full
   suite, raising bisection cost.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .` — working title
   only; the sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
   into one final commit.

### Navigating the ladder

Common moves:

- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .` — see the whole ladder
  from its base.
- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .` — jump `@` to any ladder
  commit by chid prefix; useful for bisection.
- `jj edit @-- -R .` — quick-jump back two commits.
- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .` — review one commit in
  isolation.

Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place;
descendants auto-rebase.

### Close-out: squash the ladder

When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:

```
jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
```

`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit; `-u`
keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
After squash, history is linear: `<base> -> @`;
intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.

Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit.

For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
when `@-` is `<base>`); push the single commit directly.

### Recovery

If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
prior commits:

- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
  drops it; you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
  parent.
- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
  the op history; `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
  to that point. Full undo — removes *all* ladder work
  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.

# References

- [`jj-tips.md`](jj-tips.md#revsets) — revset primitives
  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
  bisection cost.

20	  regardless of where bench threads land.
21	- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
22	  registering in `src/benches/`.
23	
24	The first benches measure Inter-Intra Application Communication
25	— function calls, async calls, channels, serde — which is what
26	seeded the project name. The harness itself is workload-agnostic.
27	The `ice-*` benches measure iceoryx2 shared-memory IPC inside one
28	process, in both of its messaging patterns (`ice-ps-*`
29	publish/subscribe, `ice-rr-*` request/response) at one and two
30	threads.
31	
32	## Design (0.2.0)
33	
34	Design a Rust app that can measure the cost of various (IIAC) techniques.
35	By IIAC I mean all communication techniques between and within
36	applications such as regular function calls vs async function calls vs
37	channels vs serde/deser of json or zero-copy messaging using io_uring and
38	potentially any other technique. It would include between threads or
39	processes or apps on the same computer or between apps on the same LAN or
40	between apps over a WAN.
41	
42	Ideally I'd like to be able to see a histogram of the range of times of the
43	send and receive costs, not just the mean/average of 10^3 or 10^6 invocations.
44	So the cost of the work should or could be something near-zero such as just
45	echoing the input, but maybe there is value in doing some constant but
46	variable amount of work to verify it's in-consequential. One thing I think we
47	need to be aware of is that if we make the work too simple the compiler could
48	just keep things in registers which would not be representative of "real" work.
49	
50	We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
51	later expand to other techniques.
52	
53	## Usage
54	
55	```
56	iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
57	iiac-perf calibrate
58	iiac-perf qualify-environment [--runs N] [--gap SECONDS] [-d SECONDS]
59	iiac-perf add-completion-yaml
60	```
61	
62	`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
63	registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
64	bench it is a prefix of — `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
65	runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the

regardless of where bench threads land.
- Plug in new workloads by implementing the `Bench` trait and
  registering in `src/benches/`.

The first benches measure Inter-Intra Application Communication
— function calls, async calls, channels, serde — which is what
seeded the project name. The harness itself is workload-agnostic.
The `ice-*` benches measure iceoryx2 shared-memory IPC inside one
process, in both of its messaging patterns (`ice-ps-*`
publish/subscribe, `ice-rr-*` request/response) at one and two
threads.

## Design (0.2.0)

Design a Rust app that can measure the cost of various (IIAC) techniques.
By IIAC I mean all communication techniques between and within
applications such as regular function calls vs async function calls vs
channels vs serde/deser of json or zero-copy messaging using io_uring and
potentially any other technique. It would include between threads or
processes or apps on the same computer or between apps on the same LAN or
between apps over a WAN.

Ideally I'd like to be able to see a histogram of the range of times of the
send and receive costs, not just the mean/average of 10^3 or 10^6 invocations.
So the cost of the work should or could be something near-zero such as just
echoing the input, but maybe there is value in doing some constant but
variable amount of work to verify it's in-consequential. One thing I think we
need to be aware of is that if we make the work too simple the compiler could
just keep things in registers which would not be representative of "real" work.

We should start simple, like comparing normal and async function calls and
later expand to other techniques.

## Usage

```
iiac-perf [BENCH...] [-d SECONDS] [-o OUTER] [-i INNER]
iiac-perf calibrate
iiac-perf qualify-environment [--runs N] [--gap SECONDS] [-d SECONDS]
iiac-perf add-completion-yaml
```

`BENCH` is one or more registered bench names, or `all` for every
registered bench. A name that matches no bench exactly runs every
bench it is a prefix of — `ice` runs all iceoryx2 benches, `mpsc`
runs `mpsc-1t` and `mpsc-2t`. **With no arguments, `iiac-perf` prints the
available list and exits — that's the source of truth for which
benches the current build registers.**

`iiac-perf calibrate` runs the startup calibration only — no
bench — and prints the
[Calibration banner](#calibration-banner) plus the raw fit
inputs: the dithered points, the three alternative fits, the
TSC tick rate, and the calibration wall time. Use it to
fingerprint a machine's frequency regime or check constant
drift without spending a bench run. The word must stand alone
(no bench names alongside); `--pin`, `--no-pin-cal`, and `-v`
apply as usual.

`iiac-perf qualify-environment` (also stand-alone) asks whether
this **machine** is fit to measure on:
it respawns this binary `--runs` times (default 10) at `--gap`
seconds apart, collects each run's environment grade, prints the
table, and gives a verdict — exiting nonzero when the machine
does not qualify. Use it to characterize a box before trusting
numbers from it.

What it runs is, in metrology terms, a repeatability study of the
apparatus plus the machine — which is why the grading module is
called `gauge`.

```
  run   warmup  env-run  worst   mean
  1     A       A        A       22.2 ns
  2     D       A        D       22.2 ns
  3     A       C        C       22.5 ns

  median environment grade: A
  transition-degraded (drift or step at D/F): 1 of 3

  verdict: NOT QUALIFIED
    a state transition landed inside a measurement window
```

It reads the environment grade rather than the run grade,
because the subject is the box: `warmup` is its settling
behaviour across respawns, `env-run` whether it then held. The
verdict is grades, not values — median at B or better, and no
run whose `drift` or `step` reached D/F, those two being the
transition detectors. `spread` and `interference` wobble is
ambient contamination and does not fail a run. The `mean` column
is informational, and it is where a two-state machine shows
itself at a glance.

Each child runs `min-now` for `-d` seconds (default 1): the box
is the subject, so the leanest bench is the right one. `--pin`
passes through to the children, and `--print-only` prints the
table without deciding a verdict.

`iiac-perf add-completion-yaml` (also stand-alone) installs the
carapace completion spec: Tab then completes bench names, command
words, and flags in any carapace-served shell — without it,
`iiac-perf ice<TAB>` has nothing to offer and bench names must
be typed (or copied from the no-args listing) by hand. Run it
once after installing iiac-perf, and again after an upgrade
that changes flags or command words; new benches never need a
re-run. See [Shell completion](#shell-completion).

Flags (also visible via `-h` / `--help`):
- `-d`, `--duration SECONDS` — target wall-clock seconds per bench
  (default `5.0`); the outer loop runs until this time is reached
  (inner auto-sizes). See chores `0.3.1-dev1` for the empirical
  study behind the default — longer (`-d 30`+) gives
  publication-grade stability. Mutually exclusive with `-D`.
- `-D`, `--total-duration SECONDS` — target total wall-clock seconds

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running
artifact. The scheme — the cycle step-numbering and the
unique-per-commit aim — is generic and shared across projects:
this file is copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
covering each medium by conditional rather than per-project
edits.

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version** — the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`),
  written with `-` in prose, ladders, chores, todo, and commit
  talk; its suffix encodes the cycle phase (see
  [Step numbering](#step-numbering)).
- **version-of-record** — the authoritative stored copy of the
  version, in the project's manifest (see
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record));
  a built or running artifact derives from it.
- **versioning** — the topic: this scheme as a whole.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and
surfaced, and how often it changes — pick the case that fits
your medium:

- **Manifest** — where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the
    committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic
    `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter, …) — add the case as
    needed
- **Notation** — how the `-` form is stored:
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`),
    store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python
    project), remap to `+` — `0.3.0-5.3.0` → `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same
    version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter** — how a built artifact surfaces the
  version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence** — how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement);
  this project follows the per-commit preference.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change
on **every commit**, so a built or running artifact identifies
the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project
  following the cycle protocol may bump less often — once per
  cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)
  if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are
  **pre-assignable**, unlike the git SHA, which a commit cannot
  contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Step numbering

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out; see
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes each commit's
phase in the version suffix — the **final identifier `0` marks
a Preparation**:

- `X.Y.Z-0` — Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, … — Work commits
- `X.Y.Z` — Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle — no ladder,
no setup commit — skips `-0` and starts at `-1` (its first
Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that
grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step without
renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10` — Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a
  Preparation.
- `-1.0` — Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final
  identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0` — Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2` — its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3` — its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0` — Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of each phase, so the
active phase is recorded — and, per the preference above,
every commit carries a distinct version.

lastPrompt: This should be it's own rung, which one, actually the "best" weould be if we did this as 0.23.1 or 0.24.0 thoughts on the mechanics of that?

content.text:
Reading versioning.md and the history changes my answer on both halves.

## Which number: 0.24.0

The history settles it. `Z` has never left `0` in this repo: 0.21.0, 0.22.0, 0.23.0, every cycle a minor bump. Choosing 0.23.1 invents a patch tier with no precedent, and it would read as "a fix to 0.23.0's feature set" when this touches no code at all. 0.24.0 follows the only pattern the repo has, and the deletion cycle then becomes 0.25.0.

Worth noting: versioning.md specifies the *suffix* in detail and says nothing about how `X.Y.Z` advances. So this is an unrecorded convention we are deciding by precedent, not a rule we are following.

## The mechanics problem, and it is a real one

A cycle's close-out must be its last commit, and the sweep is sitting in `@` right now. That means whatever commits next commits next, so there are only three ways to give the sweep its own `X.Y.Z`, and one is invalid:

- **Interleaving is out.** 0.23.0-6 → 0.24.0 → back to 0.23.0-7 moves the version-of-record backwards. That breaks the single property versioning.md actually asserts, that a running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from, and it makes `-V` ambiguous about ordering.
- **jj surgery.** `jj commit` the sweep as S, then `jj new -B S` to insert the close-out beneath it and let S auto-rebase. This works, but it will conflict in `TODO.md`: the close-out deletes the `## In Progress` block that the sweep just rewrote line by line. Hand-resolvable, and the resolution is "drop those hunks," but it is a conflict you would be resolving for no gain.
- **Drop the entangled part instead.** This is the one I would do, and it costs nothing real.

## Recommended sequence

The insight that makes it cheap: about 60 of the sweep's `TODO.md` conversions are inside the `## In Progress` ladder, and close-out *deletes* that block, migrating it into `chores-05.md`'s As-built section. So that work was always going to be thrown away by the very next commit.

1. **Revert only the ladder portion** of the `TODO.md` sweep. Keep the `## Todo` / `## Ideas` / `## Done` conversions, which survive close-out.
2. **Bare `0.23.0` close-out.** Bookkeeping only, as the protocol requires: move the item to `## Done`, migrate the ladder into `chores-05.md`, retire the block. The ladder arrives in chores with its original dashes, which is fine because step 3 fixes it.
3. **`0.24.0` docs cycle**, a lightweight one with no `-0`: the sweep of `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, `cycle-protocol.md`, and `TODO.md`'s surviving sections, plus a pass over the As-built text that just landed in `chores-05.md`. That last part is "existing text converts when touched," and it means the migrated ladder ends up converted anyway, in its permanent home rather than in the block that was about to disappear.
4. **`0.25.0`** for `refactor: drop overhead calibration`.

Promoting the deletion to its own cycle is independently right, not just a consequence. Its precondition is already satisfied: the environment certificate landed at -6, so build-then-demolish is met. It is a pure deletion with its own risk profile, and 0.23.0's ladder is eight rungs deep already.

## Two things this turned up

- **versioning.md is itself full of banned characters** and is explicitly "copied verbatim" across projects. Sweeping it locally would fork the template. The right move is upstreaming the rule to `vc-template-x1`, which is close kin to the existing "Upstream the ladder commit-ref convention" Todo. I would leave versioning.md alone and add that to the Todo list rather than diverge it.
- **The `X.Y.Z` advancement convention should get written down**, since we just decided it by reading git log. versioning.md is the natural home but is verbatim-shared, so it needs a project-specific location. That is a question for you.

**The plain version:** call it 0.24.0, because this project has only ever counted by the middle number and 0.23.1 would invent a new kind of release. The awkward bit is that the current cycle is not finished, and you cannot slot a new version in front of unfinished work without the numbers going backwards. The fix is easy though: most of my TODO.md edits were to a section that the next commit deletes anyway, so I throw those away, finish the current cycle, and then do the sweep as its own 0.24.0 with the deleted text cleaned up where it lands instead.

content.text:
**12 inbound links, across 3 files:**

- `notes/cycle-protocol.md` — 7 (lines 11, 20, 24, 115, 120, 180, 244)
- `notes/README.md` — 4 (lines 68, 72, 74, 76)
- `AGENTS.md` — 1 (line 692)

Plus one prose mention in `notes/chores/chores-03.md:734`, historical, not a link.

## Pushback: only one of its five sections is the noise you're describing

You are right about **Recording the version-of-record**. That is ~27 of 105 lines spent on `if Rust / if Python / if TOML bars a hyphen` conditionals, and for this repo it reduces to one sentence: `Cargo.toml [package].version`, surfaced by `iiac-perf -V`. Dead weight.

But the other three sections are load-bearing and are not derivable from `Cargo.toml`:

- **Step numbering** — the whole `-0` Preparation / `-N` Work / bare Close-out scheme, nesting (`-3.1.0`), the disambiguation that `-10` is Work #10 while `-1.0` is a sub-cycle Preparation, and optional-Preparation. `cycle-protocol.md:177-181` explicitly delegates here: *"The full scheme ... lives in versioning.md, which is the single source of truth for this repo's versioning."* Delete the file and that section points at nothing, and the suffix spec is gone from the repo.
- **Unique per commit** — the policy that the version bumps on *every* commit. That is why `Cargo.toml` currently reads `0.23.0-6` and not `0.23.0`. `Cargo.toml` shows the current value; it cannot tell you the cadence that produced it.
- **Terms** — `version` / `version-of-record` / `versioning` as used verbatim across AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md.

## What I would do instead: absorb, then delete

Fold Terms, Unique-per-commit, and Step numbering into `cycle-protocol.md`'s `## Numbering`, which today is a 9-line stub whose only job is delegating outward. Collapse Recording to a single line. Then delete `versioning.md` and repoint the 12 links.

Net effect: one fewer file, the same content, one fewer hop when reading, and `## Numbering` becomes self-contained instead of a redirect. It also dissolves the exemption I flagged last turn, since once the text is local rather than verbatim-shared it simply gets swept with everything else.

**One thing to weigh before deciding.** The file's header says it is copied **verbatim** across projects from the template, with per-medium variation handled by conditional rather than local edits. Deleting it here is a deliberate fork from `vc-template-x1`. If you want the template to keep carrying this scheme, then the local move is "absorb and delete here, and upstream the same restructuring to the template" rather than a quiet local deletion. That pairs naturally with the "Upstream the ladder commit-ref convention" Todo, which is already about pushing conventions back to that repo.

**The plain version:** twelve links point at it, mostly from cycle-protocol.md. You are right that the part explaining *where* the version is stored is pointless for a Rust project, but the file also defines the `-0`, `-1`, `-2` numbering scheme and the rule that every commit bumps the version, and cycle-protocol.md tells the reader to go there for it. So rather than deleting outright, move those two bits into cycle-protocol.md and then delete the file. Same simplification you want, without losing the scheme.

message.content: Just thinking, what if versioning.md information when directly into AGENTS and/or cycle-protocol and in README.md we tell the user to choose a technique and then delete that section from the README.md when chosen?

content.text:
Good instinct, and it resolves the "and/or" if you sort by **lifetime** rather than by topic. The file mixes two kinds of text:

- **Decided once, then never read again** — which manifest, hyphen-vs-plus notation, how the artifact reports its version. Onboarding text.
- **Read every cycle, forever** — Terms, the per-commit bump policy, `-0`/`-N`/bare, nesting, `-10` vs `-1.0`.

That mixture *is* why the file reads as noise: 27 lines of one-time setup sitting in a doc you consult mid-cycle. Splitting them is the fix, and your self-deleting section is the right shape for the first kind.

## Where each half goes, decided by sharing model

The "and/or" answers itself once you notice that AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md have different sharing models:

- **cycle-protocol.md is generic/shared** (its intro literally says "substitute your medium's equivalents"). So the *generic scheme* goes there, absorbed into `## Numbering`, which today is a 9-line stub whose only job is redirecting to versioning.md. It becomes self-contained.
- **AGENTS.md is per-project adapted** (it carries repo paths, the `code` scope name, things vc-x1's copy spells differently). So the *project's actual choice* goes there, in the `**Versioning.**` paragraph at line 692 that already exists as the project-facing pointer. It changes from "see versioning.md" to one line: manifest is `Cargo.toml [package].version`, surfaced by `iiac-perf -V`.

That way neither doc gets a fact whose lifetime doesn't match it, and nothing project-specific lands in a verbatim-shared file.

## On the self-deleting section: right idea, wrong README for this repo

Two things to separate:

- **This repo's `README.md` is the product's user-facing doc** — usage, flags, band tables, for someone benchmarking. Bot-facing setup instructions do not belong in it. And iiac-perf's choice was made long ago, so there is nothing here to choose and nothing to delete. The section should simply never exist in this repo.
- **`vc-template-x1`'s README is where it belongs**, because that is the only place a reader is actually making the choice. Pairs directly with the existing "Upstream the ladder commit-ref convention" Todo.

**The failure mode to design against:** a "delete this when done" section that nobody deletes is exactly the stale noise you are removing, now shipped into every clone. Three cheap defenses, in increasing strength:

- Put the instruction in the heading, so staleness is visible at a glance: `## Setup: choose your versioning technique (delete this section when done)`.
- Make the deletion a numbered step in the template's setup checklist, so it is a task rather than a hope.
- Add a `vc-x1 validate-repo` check: if a manifest exists and the setup section is still present, warn. AGENTS.md already anticipates `validate-repo` for dangling anchors and title-vs-commit mismatches, so this is one more rule in a checker that is coming anyway. This is the one that actually holds.

## Net result

`versioning.md` deleted, 12 links repointed (7 in cycle-protocol.md become internal `#numbering` links, 4 in notes/README.md, 1 in AGENTS.md), no content lost, one fewer hop for a reader, and the template keeps the scheme. It also improves the sweep story: cycle-protocol.md is already in the swept set, so the absorbed text gets converted as it lands rather than needing a second pass.

Scope-wise this is its own cycle, not a rung of the docs sweep. I would sequence it after 0.24.0 rather than folding it in, since it is a structural change to three files plus a deletion, and mixing it into a punctuation sweep would make both diffs hard to review.

That split actually removes a question from the plan rather than complicating it: **version-of-record is a work-repo concept**, since the bot repo is a linear journal with no manifest and no version. So the absorbed scheme, the setup section, and the `validate-repo` check all land in `vc-x1-work-repo-template`, with nothing for the bot-repo template to carry.

Here is the rename's blast radius in this repo, sorted by whether it should change:

**Should update (3 live sites):**

- `TODO.md:375` — the upstreaming Todo's `../vc-template-x1`. Its line 378 also lists "the template's cycle-protocol.md, AGENTS.md, and TODO.md", which now wants to name the work-repo template explicitly.
- `AGENTS.md:789` — "vc-template-x1 template's `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml`". `CargoRust.toml` is work-repo by nature, so this becomes the work-repo template.
- `notes/jj-tips.md:16` — `jj git remote add origin git@github.com:winksaville/vc-template-x1`, inside a "minimal commands to push" recipe meant to be copied. I would make it `winksaville/<repo>` rather than pick either new name, since the recipe is about the command shape and any real name there will go stale again.

**Should not update (leave as-is):**

- `notes/jj-tips.md:35-154` — pasted shell transcripts, complete with prompts, timestamps, and bookmark state. Transcribed output.
- `notes/done.md:74-75` and `notes/chores/chores-04.md:211, 217, 614, 637` — historical records of work done *when the repo was named that*. Renaming them would make the record wrong about its own past.

That split falls out of the exemption we just finished writing, which is a useful sign it was worth the argument: "transcribed, not written" and "already-published" cover a rename just as well as they cover punctuation. The principle generalizes past the case it was written for.

**Sequencing.** These three edits are a rename, not a punctuation conversion, so folding them into the 0.24.0 sweep would put two unrelated kinds of change in one diff. content.text:
Measured, and the rebase is not a hassle — the overlap is far smaller than I assumed:

| file | changed lines | lines in -7's blast zone |
|---|---:|---:|
| `AGENTS.md` | 300 | 0 |
| `notes/cycle-protocol.md` | 200 | 0 |
| `README.md` | 274 | 10 |
| `TODO.md` | 245 | the ladder only |

`-7` deletes `overhead.rs`, the constants block, the adjusted columns and the `calibrate` command, so it touches README's calibration prose and nothing else. Only 10 of my 274 README lines sit in that zone, and AGENTS.md and cycle-protocol.md are untouched by anything left in 0.23.0.

**So: branch it, don't redo.** Redoing means re-making roughly 360 hand judgments about commas versus parentheses versus sub-bullets, and they would come out subtly different from these, which makes the eventual review harder rather than easier. The mechanical third of the sweep is scriptable; the em dash prose is not, and that is where the work actually went.

Both conflicts resolve by *deleting* my hunks, which is the cheap kind:

- **TODO.md ladder** — close-out removes the whole `## In Progress` block, so those hunks just drop. The text reappears in `chores-05.md`'s As-built section, where I convert it as part of the sweep cycle.
- **README calibration prose** — `-7` deletes those sections outright, so same story for most of the 10 lines.

## Mechanics

1. `jj commit` the sweep now, then `jj bookmark create punctuation-sweep -r @-`. Cheap insurance and it gets the work out of the working copy.
2. `jj new <main-tip>` to fork back to main for `-7` and the close-out. The sweep commit sits off to the side on its bookmark.
3. After 0.23.0 closes: `jj rebase -b punctuation-sweep -d main`, resolve the two files, then `jj describe` and bump `Cargo.toml`.
4. Escape hatch if the README conflict turns out uglier than predicted: `jj squash --from <sweep> --into @ AGENTS.md notes/cycle-protocol.md` moves only the clean files, and I re-sweep README fresh against post-`-7` text. `jj squash` takes paths, so the split costs one command.

**Two details worth deciding now:**

- **No `Cargo.toml` bump in the sweep commit today.** It cannot know its own version until 0.23.0 closes, so the bump belongs in step 3's `describe`, not now. The branch commit stays docs-only.
- **`-7` lands before the rule does.** So when I write `-7`'s new README sentence about apparatus framing, I should write it dash-free from the start, otherwise the sweep has to come back and catch text that was authored after the convention was agreed but before it was committed.

One flag: you said 0.23.1 here, and earlier we landed on 0.24.0 on the grounds that `Z` has never left `0` in this repo's history, so a patch number would invent a tier. I do not think it matters much, but I would rather ask than silently pick. **0.24.0 or 0.23.1?**

**The plain version:** keep the work on a branch and rebase it later. I checked, and the current cycle's remaining work barely touches the same lines, so the rebase should be nearly clean, and the few clashes are places where the other commit deletes the text anyway. Redoing the sweep by hand would be hundreds of small judgment calls again for no benefit. I just need to know whether you want it numbered 0.24.0 or 0.23.1.

This is the repo's first non-functional cycle, which makes it the first legitimate `.1` rather than an invented tier. **0.23.1 it is** — and that decision is exactly the unrecorded `X.Y.Z` convention worth writing down when versioning.md gets absorbed.

One correction to my own step 3 before I park anything, because it walks into a bug this repo has already been bitten by. `cycle-protocol.md:553-564` records that `vc-x1 push` *creates* the commit from pending changes and does not publish an already-committed shape — at the 0.22.0 close-out that minted an empty stamped commit on the old tip. So a pre-committed sweep must be folded **back into the working copy** at revival, not pushed as-is. That makes this a parking commit that gets squashed away, which per AGENTS.md means no `ochid:` on it now.
